newsitem.title: IRAQ: CIA spies shown on Iraqi tv, US disputes claim.
newsitem.headline: CIA spies shown on Iraqi tv, US disputes claim.

text.p: Iraqi television on Friday showed four Iraqis who confessed to spying for the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency but in Washington officials dismissed Baghdad's claims of having uncovered a CIA spy network.
Saad Daham Awad, 32, an officer in the Iraqi army, appeared on state-run Iraqi television on Friday evening and explained in a relaxed manner how he was recruited to spy for the CIA.

Awad, wearing civilian clothes, said he was approached in northern Iraq by a Kurd, whom he named as Howker Ahmed Ali, working for the CIA's Iraq Trust group that used as its cover building hospitals and schools in the area.
He later recruited his brother Salahuddin, who appeared on the programme along with two other Iraqis who also confessed to spying.
The Kurdish north has been under the control of the Kurds since after the 1991 Gulf War, and the region is protected from Iraqi forces by a U.S.-led air operation.
Awad said he began smuggling medicine from Baghdad to the north and later started turning over information on the Iraqi army.
"Howker asked me to write a detailed report on the Iraqi military security office. I wrote the report and he paid me 150,000 Iraqi dinars (about $120) after giving him a receipt," Awad said.
"The Iraq Trust group is known publicly as building schools and hospitals but in reality it belongs to the CIA with an office in Zakho (in north Iraq)," he said.
He added that the group was headed by Howker's brother Haiman.

The Iraqi TV presenter accused the U.S. administration of carrying espionage actions against Iraq under the cover of humanitarian organisations. "These non-governmental humanitarian agencies are used by the U.S. administration as a cover for its CIA activities," the presenter said.
"America and Zionism (Israel) have not only launched military, economic and political wars against Iraq but they went too far to destroy the will of some Iraqis of weak souls," he said.
Awad said that he had been caught by Iraqi intelligence officers but did not say when that had happened.
"The Iraqi intelligence officers were following my activities and when they caught me they took me to the place where I used to hide the code (of spying)," he said.
Iraqi television showed two more confessed spies,Mahamoud Abdulkhaliq and Sartib Hilmi, described as taxi drivers.

Abdulkhaliq said he had been asked by Howker to collect information from people who hired his taxi in Baghdad about the general situation in Iraq while Hilmi was to transport letters between Awad, Howker and Haiman.

At the end of the programme the presenter warned viewers not to commit crimes similar to those of Awad and his group and urged them to tell the authorities if they were ever approached by anyone to carry out espionage acts.
He also urged anyone involved in spying to report this to the authorities, as this would help minimise their punishments.
The programme failed to say what punishment the four who appeared on televison were facing.
A CIA spokesman in the United States declined to comment on the report but U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the Iraqi charges were merely propaganda.

"Frankly, if anybody believes these reports they ought to have their heads examined. This is a well-noted and tired propaganda ploy," Burns told a news briefing before Awad appeared on Iraqi television.

Iraqi dissident groups in Europe have said that, when the Iraqi troops entered the north earlier this year, they broke up a long-standing CIA-funded covert operation to destabilise Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
This is not the first time Iraq has accused the United States, which led the allied force that drove Iraq out of Kuwait in 1991, of recruiting agents to carry out acts of sabotage.
Last March Baghdad said the United States had recruited agents who planted car bombs in the capital Baghdad, Tikrit and other Iraqi cities.
In the same month Iraq also accused Gulf War foe Kuwait of recruiting agents who carried out sabotage attacks against the Iraqi people, U.N. observers and arms inspectors.
Iraq's state-run television then interviewed six Iraqis from Basra who said the Kuwaiti secret police had recruited them to plant bombs in various parts of the country.
